France: on the eve of a general strike, five unions and young people march Thursday against the cost of living

On Thursday 5 November, the CFDT, CGT, FO, Unsa and FSU have called a day of strikes and demonstrations, after weeks of mobilisation by high-school and university students. Wages, public services and jobs are at the heart of the demands; trains and schools will be disrupted [1][2][3].

The inter-union alliance (CFDT, CGT, FO, Unsa, FSU) is calling on private- and public-sector workers to strike and march on Thursday 5 November, with demands on wages, public services, jobs and industry, AFP reports [1]. The CGT also wants a different state and social security budget [1].

According to an internal Interior Ministry note cited by L'Express and Orange, 500,000 to 700,000 demonstrators are expected in the regions. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez called it a "sensitive" day [3].

At SNCF, the CGT, Unsa ferroviaire, SUD-Rail and the CFDT have filed a 24-hour strike notice over pay and jobs. A meeting with management on Tuesday 3 November did not defuse the dispute. SNCF expects "slightly disrupted" TGV traffic and "disrupted" Intercités and TER services; one TER in two will run in Hauts-de-France [2]. In Île-de-France, the RATP expects normal traffic, while RER B will be disrupted [2].
In Lyon, metro lines B, C and D and the two funiculars will be shut all day [3].

High-school and university students, already in the streets for several weeks, are blockading schools and universities on Tuesday and Thursday, according to franceinfo; the gilets jaunes coordination is calling for a "people's 5 November" [1][4].
Key point: after weeks of youth mobilisation, the employee unions are taking over, according to AFP. The common theme is the cost of living: when prices rise faster than wages, demands converge [1].

The date is no accident. The National Assembly is examining the 2027 budget, in which the government wants big savings, and it has not managed to vote on the revenue part (see our brief today). The unions want to weigh in before the vote [1][4].

For the government the risk is twofold: a black Thursday in transport, then a movement that settles in. According to the CGT, the Prime Minister has not yet announced a date to receive youth organisations [4].

If you are taking a train on Thursday, check your journey: one TER in two in Hauts-de-France, disrupted Intercités. If you are a student, blockades may close your school. In Paris, metro and buses should run normally.

EU enlargement: Montenegro aims for 2028, Ukraine sees Hungary giving way, Georgia stays stuck

On 3 November in Brussels, the Euronews Enlargement Summit showed a multi-speed club: Montenegro, Albania and Moldova are advancing, Ukraine hopes to open its last two negotiating clusters before year-end, while Georgia offered no way out of its crisis [1][2][3].

Montenegro aims to join in 2028 as the EU's 28th member. Its European Affairs Minister, Maida Gorčević, warned that her country will not accept "second-class" membership; according to Euronews, its progress is slowed by bilateral disputes with Croatia, inherited from the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s [1].

Ukraine's envoy to the EU, Taras Kachka, told Euronews that Hungary has "no new substantive objections" to opening the last two negotiating clusters, 4 and 5, which he hopes to see opened by the end of 2026. For him, the word "blocking" is misleading: Budapest mainly wants time to study the documents [3].

The EU opened clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine in October, in Luxembourg. Kachka keeps the goal of finishing negotiations in 2027 or 2028, or even earlier if reforms go faster than expected [3]. Euronews links this progress to the change of government in Hungary [1].

But the Ukrinform agency recalls that at Council working-group meetings on 20 and 27 October, Hungary refused to approve the screening conclusions for clusters 4 and 5, although it had lifted its objections on two others [4]. The two readings are therefore not yet settled.

In Georgia, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said he remains committed to accession, but blamed the European Commission and refused to revisit the controversial laws that froze the candidacy. He called Brussels' assessment false and akin to political blackmail [2]. In November 2024, Tbilisi had announced it would not seek to open negotiations before the end of 2028 [2].
Armenia opened another door: its Prime Minister called a formal application in 2027 or 2028 "realistic" [1].

Key point: enlargement is no longer a slogan, it is a timetable. Montenegro (2028) and Ukraine (negotiations finished in 2027-2028) give dates, which forces the EU to settle its own questions: budget, agriculture, the right of veto [1][3].

Hungary was the main lock for Kyiv. If its new government lifts its objections, Ukraine can move fast; if the refusal of 20 and 27 October is confirmed, Kachka's timetable slips [3][4]. According to Euronews, Ukraine also rejected agricultural carve-outs to its accession [1].

Enlargement also depends on the Twenty-Seven's own politics: Croatia's Prime Minister warned that the French presidential election, with the rise of Eurosceptic forces, could derail the process [1]. For the rest of the region, Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos reportedly spoke of countries that are "candidates only on paper" [1].

If you live in the EU, new members would mostly affect agriculture and the EU budget: Ukrainians have already rejected agricultural exceptions, and member states are negotiating how to split the funds of the next 2028-2034 budget.

news.2026-11-04-france-budget-2027-vote-: France: the vote on 2027 budget revenues did not take place, as amendments were not finished

The solemn vote on the "revenue" part of the 2027 budget, planned for Tuesday 3 November at the National Assembly, was postponed: MPs had not finished examining the amendments. With no majority for Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, a rejection is seen as likely and 49.3 is being discussed [1][2][3].
The vote planned for Tuesday afternoon did not take place because the "marathon" on the revenue part was not over, LCP reports [1]. It is the second postponement, after 20 October [1].

In the chamber, David Amiel, Minister for Public Accounts, defended a €5.5 billion levy on local authorities as imperative, and blamed MPs for worsening the planned deficit by €10 billion through their amendments, according to La Gazette des communes [3].
LCP considers it "more than likely" that the revenue part will be rejected, for lack of a majority, as the social security budget was [1].
If the vote fails, the government can use Article 49.3 or, after the constitutional deadlines, ordinances under Article 47, Public Sénat explains [2].
Key point: France enters November without the revenue part of the budget voted, and without a clear majority to pass it [1][2].
The deadlock feeds social anger: unions want a different budget, and the 5 November strike falls in the middle of the debate [2].
An unvoted budget changes nothing in your pay tomorrow, but it will decide your taxes and benefits in 2027: follow the rest of the debate at the Assembly.
Examination of the amendments resumes; the government keeps 49.3 and ordinances in reserve [2].
